austere

aw-STEER -- from Greek austeros, 'harsh, dry, bitter,' first said of taste and later of people. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Austere is severe or strict in manner, or stripped down to plain essentials.

The judge's austere expression gave no hint of what she was thinking.

Example

A retired teacher lives in an austere single room with a cot, a lamp, one chair, and a shelf of books, and gives away anything she has not used in a year.

A life stripped down to strict, plain essentials is what makes the room austere. Unlike 'poor,' which is forced on someone, austere often names a severity that a person chooses.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stern: Stern describes a manner -- serious, unsmiling, firm -- and only a manner. A stern librarian may still go home to a cozy, cluttered apartment. Austere reaches further: an austere person carries severity into a whole way of life, and austere can also describe rooms, styles, and budgets stripped to essentials.

strict: Strict means demanding exact obedience to rules -- a strict coach runs every drill by the book. It is about controlling conduct, usually someone else's. Austere is about severity of style and living: an austere room enforces nothing on anyone; it simply does without every comfort and ornament.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

lavish: rich and generously supplied

indulgent: freely allowing comfort and pleasure

Where it sits · how little comfort or softness remains

plain → austere → spartan

plain vs. austere: Plain is much milder than austere -- a plain room just skips decoration, while an austere one strips away comfort itself, down to bare essentials.

spartan vs. austere: Spartan is austere at its most extreme: an austere room is plain, while a spartan room offers nothing beyond bare survival -- named for the ancient Spartans, who trained themselves to need almost nothing.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — austere: harsh, bitter, dry (Greek (austeros), via Latin austerus)

Put it together: Greek austeros first described a taste -- dry, bitter, and sharp on the tongue -- and Latin borrowed it as austerus. English carried the word from bitter flavors to bitter manners, so an austere person is 'harsh to the taste' in the way they treat others. The same root gives us austerity.

Use the root in a new word: austerity: The finance minister spent the whole interview defending her austerity plan without once raising her voice.

Word Building

Word Choice

Austere works in two registers that the ISEE treats as one word: a person can be austere (severe, strict, unsmiling) and so can a place or a style (bare, plain, undecorated). Both come from the same idea of harsh simplicity.
